tei:div.tei:note: The lesson reports for Gerhard Alberesheim in the original are written continuously, without paragraph breaks or separating punctuation. They have been separated here in the interests of legibility.
tei:div.tei:ab: 3. X. Fragen zu Beethovens Klaviersonaten u. Streichquartett op. 181.
7. op. 81a als Hauptstudium.Diary October 7, 1927: “Albersheim has still not paid – I write him a recommendation for Buxbaum regarding a subscription to the Philharmonic concerts.”
10. Zu Beethoven op. 181.
14. Generalbaß begonnen.

17. Fragen zu Beethoven 591, Form;– zu Figaros Hochzeit (Vorhalte).Presumably the suspensions and their resolutions in one of the numbers from the opera, for instance, the bass notes in bars 3, 5, 6, and 7 in the opening duet “Cinque… dieci…”
21. Zu Beyschlags Ornamentik;Adolf Beyschlag, Ornamentik der Musik (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1908). Beethoven 185 (Rosé’s Vortrag); zu Schuberts Hm-Sinfonie.

24. Wolf „Italienische Serenade“; Brahms’ Sonate op. 5; Beethoven 591 u. 2; Reger Streichquartett Andante Adur mit VariationenReger’s String Quartet Op. 54, No. 2, in A major; the second movement is an Andante with variations, in D major. op. 81a, 1. Satz abgeschlossen.
28. Einiges zur Walküre; zu Brahms op. 1171 Vortrag.
31. Zu 592, 3; u. Harfen-Quartett.
4. XI. Musikgeschichtliches u. Zukunftsbetrachtungen in historischem Zusammenhang.
7. Metrisches zu 592, 3.
11. S. Bach Suite Edur begonnen, Bilder zur Allemande.

18. Zu
Beethovens Bläserquintett, Form u. Vortrag;There are no works by Beethoven in the traditional wind quintet scoring; Schenker is probably referring to the Quintet in E for piano and wind instruments, Op. 16. zu Beethovens 95 Form.
21. Allemande, letzte Hintergrundbilder u. Vortrag.Diary November 21, 1927: “Albersheim asks for a fourth [weekly] lesson – if it is possible for me.”

25. Brahms 1075 „Mädchenlied“, Linie korrigiert; Götterdämmerung Seite 213 (?), Tonarten – Fragen.Possibly p. 213 of the piano-vocal score edited by Felix Mottl (Leipzig: Peters, c. 1914), where Brünnhilde sings “Heißet Brünnhild, ihr Herz zu verbrechen” and the orchestra plays a version of the “Sleep” motive from Act III of Die Walküre.
28. Zu Beethovens op. 127 Esdur.

2. XII. Ueber Mayerbeer’s Prophet; zu Beethovens Streichquartett Bdur; zeigt einen Aufsatz von Reichwein in der Kölner Musik-Ztg.Diary December 3, 1927: “I work on Beethoven's Quartet in C minor for Albersheim.”

5. Ueber Klaiber (in Anschluß an das Strauß-KonzertA concert by the Vienna Philharmonic under Erich Kleiber took place on Sunday December 4, 1927. It was not, however, a Strauss concert: the program comprised works by Purcell, Glazunov, and Mahler.); Courante begonnen.Diary December 4, 1927: “I work on Bach-Schemelli Nos. 1 and 8 for Albersheim.”

9. Schemelli-Roth No 1Herman Roth, ed., 25 Geistliche Lieder (aus dem Schemellischen Gesangbuch) für eine Singstimme und basso continuo (Leipzig: C. F. Peters, [n.d.]), a copy of which, with annotations in Schenker's hand, is preserved at OJ 25/1; No. 1 “Auf, auf! die rechte Zeit ist hier” (BWV 440). corrigiert.Diary December 9, 1927: “Albersheim does not appear until 11 o'clock, instead of at 10 – I give him 50 shillings back and decide to refuse giving him the fourth lesson – he, at any rate, would like to make a misunderstanding responsible. I, however, look at the matter more deeply and choose not to give the lesson, and indeed as punishment for the deception, since it was he who asked me for the fourth lesson and added that his father had authorized it – it is impossible for an agreement to be solicited and granted in respect of a single lesson; it would have to apply to the continuous arrangement of a fourth lesson.”

12. Schemelli-Roth No 8Herman Roth, ed., 25 Geistliche Lieder (aus dem Schemellischen Gesangbuch) für eine Singstimme und basso continuo (Leipzig: C. F. Peters, [n.d.]), a copy of which, with annotations in Schenker's hand, is preserved at OJ 25/1; No. 8 “Jesu, deine Liebeswunden” (BWV 471).; Sarabande begonnen.Diary December 12, 1927: “I cancel Albersheim's fourth weekly lesson.”
16. Choral „Herzliebster Jesu“ aus der Matthäuspassion Hmoll.

19. 2. Fassung, s. Erk,Presumably the second version of the chorale “Herzliebster Jesu” from the St. Matthew Passion; see lessonbook entry for December 16. dazu Choräle von Mendelssohn u. a. (Sammlung Peters); Choralvorspiele u. Fantasien von S. Bach, s. Orgelwerke; Gavotte begonnen.

23. Generalbaß beendet; Chopin Polonaise begonnen; aus Figaros Hochzeit
Cherubin-Arie,Schenker does not specify whether this was “Non so più” (Act 1) or “Voi che sapete” (Act 2). Bild corrigirt.

30. Motette BdurEither Bach’s “Singet dem Herrn,” BWV 225, or “Der Geist hilft unser Schwachheit auf,” BWV 226, both of which are in B major. begonnen, Bilder dazu.Diary December 30, 1927: “Albersheim asks me to send a letter of recommendation to Walter.” — Diary January 1, 1928: “I work on the motet and suite for Albersheim.” — January 15, 1928: “In the evening, work on the motet for Albersheim.”

9. I. Gigue begonnen, somit die Suite beendet.Diary January 9, 1928: “From Albersheim (express postcard): he was received by Walter and favored with an acceptance; his postcard arrived late, A. was already with me when it arrived; A. asks again for the second Friday lesson; I decline.”

13. Zum Besuch bei Heger u. dessen Urteil.Diary January 3, 1928: “From Albersheim (express letter): should he go to [Robert] Heger, to whom Dr. Bienenfeld has recommended him, in order to play to him, and should he take a letter of reference to Walter?” — January 5, 1928: “From Albersheim (postcard): he cannot see Heger until next week. — To Albersheim (express postcard): I shall write to Walter today.” Mozart alla turca, Linie corrigirt.
16. krank.Diary Jan 19, 1928: “From Albersheim (postcard): unwell, stays home, out of consideration for me.”
19. krank.

23. In die MotetteEither Bach’s “Singet dem Herrn,” BWV 225, or “Der Geist hilft unser Schwachheit auf,” BWV 226. Vortrag eingezeichnet gemäß dem Ergebnis der Linien.Diary January 23, 1928: “After a lengthy illness, Albersheim reappears.”

27. Zu Schuberts Streichquartett Gdur Andante music exampleA (rhythmically inaccurate) quotation of the pair of notes G-natural–B which interrupt the chromatic descent in bars 55–57. Ornamente bei Schubert.

30. Ueber Antisemitismus, offenbar eine Krise in seinem Liebesverhältnis.Diary Jan 30, 1928, begins: “Albersheim, visibly caught in a crisis, brings up the matter of the justification of anti-Semitism and remains uneasy for two hours; only towards the end of the second hour could I understand him: his girlfriend, who comes from an aristocratic officers' circle, is full of prejudice against the Jews. [...]”
3. II. Ornamentik bei S. Bach, Fragen zu meiner Ornamentik.
10. Zu Beethovens Streichquartett 135, Fragen; zu Joh Strauß’ „An der schönen blauen Donau“, Linien.
13. MotetteEither Bach’s “Singet dem Herrn,” BWV 225, or “Der Geist hilft unser Schwachheit auf,” BWV 226. beendet.
17. Fuge Emoll, I, mit Bild; zu Schuberts Klaviersonaten, Formfragen.

20. Zu Stellen aus der kleinen Monographie von Siegfried Ochs über
den Chor.Probably Siegfried Ochs, Über die Art, Musik zu hören (Berlin: Werk Verlag, 1926), which is just 54 pages long.

24. Fuge Dmoll I; zu Em. Bachs Manieren, Mordent u. Anschlag; zum Vortrag der Suite Fragen gestellt u. fortlaufend methodisch beantwortet.Diary Feb 15, 1928: “I work on the Fugue in E minor from Book I (for Albersheim).” — Feb 18, 1928: “I work on fugue and prelude (for Albersheim).”

27. Aus Carmen, Vortrag einiger Stellen; über Hörner u. Trompeten überhaupt; zu Furtwänglers Vortrag der III. Sinf. v. Brahms; zu Berlioz’ Symphonie phantastique; Vortrag der Fugen Cm I, Dm I, Em I, dazu Präludien Cm u. Em.

2. III. Em. Bach: Fragen zu den Manieren u. zum Abschnitt Vortrag.C. P. E. Bach, Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, transl. & ed. William J. Mitchell (New York: Norton, 1949), pp. 366–79.

5. Brandenburgische Konzert Ddur begonnen, Linie des 1. Satzes.Diary Jan 8, 1928: “I work on the Brandenburg Concerto in D major for Albersheim.” — March 6: “Work on the Brandenburg Concerto, second movement (for Albersheim).” — March: “Work on the Brandenburg Concerto, last movement; Albersheim asks for the fourth lesson.”
12. Auch Fingersatz u. Vortrag der Suite abgeschlossen. Continuo zum 1. Satz des Brandenburgischen Konzerts corrigirt; zu Mozarts Sinfonie Ddur 3sätzig.

19. Hat wieder einmal gefehlt! Beethovens Scherzo Skizze , zur VIII. Sinfonie (Heck) erläutert; Brandenburgisches Konzert, 2. Satz, Linie;
Beethoven Quintett Cdur: Form des letzten Satzes.
23. Continuo zum 2. Satz.Diary March 22: “I work on the Brandenburg Concerto (for Albersheim).”
26. Linie zum 3. Satz.

2. IV. Aus Em. Bachs letzten Abschnitt über die Vorschläge. Brahms’ Sextett Gdur; ob der diagram of a mordent im Scherzo vorher oder auf dem Kopf zu spielen ist. Ueber Stellen im Weihnachts-Oratorium von S. Bach, Deklamationsfragen (Ausgleich von stark u. schwach durch Quantität).Diary March 30, 1928: “Albersheim surprises me with his wish to remain in Vienna, on condition of the approval of his father. He would be prepared to be educated further, in order to decide then between a conducting and a teaching career. Concerning the question of whether I would be prepared to support his petition to his father, I agree, on condition that he provide me in advance with the assurance that his father does not suspect me of a dishonorable financial arrangement.” — April 2, 1928: “Albersheim announces to me that his father will come in May [see May 25], then it should be decided about further continuation.”

6. Brandenburgisches Konzert: Vortrag des 1. Satzes für das Nicolai Konzert.“Nicolai Concert”: an annual concert given by the Vienna Philharmonic in honor of the orchestra’s founder, Otto Nicolai (1810–49). Wilhelm Furtwängler conducted the concert on Sunday April 15, 1928, in a program comprising Bruckner’s Symphony No. 7 and Bach’s Brandenburg Concerto No. 5 with Furtwängler as keyboard soloist.
13. Vortrag des 2. u. 3. Satzes.
16. Ueber Furtwänglers Vortrag des Brandenburgischen Konzertes; Linie des 1. Satzes corrig.
20. Fragen zu Bachs Johannes-Passion; zu Smetana „Die verkaufte Braut“, 8–8 Stelle; über Smetana u. Dvořak überhaupt.

23. Zu Variationen-Werken von Schubert in Litolff III; S. Bach: Arie Ddur aus einer
Cantate, Linie u. Vortrag.
25. (statt 18. VI): Fragen zu Brahms’ Sextett; noch einmal die Linie zu 81a, 1. Satz durchgegangen u. verbessert.
27. Zur Linzer Sinfonie von Mozart, Cdur, auch vierhändig gespielt.
30. Zu 81a noch einmal die Linie des Andante; mit dem genauen Studium des Vortrags methodisch begonnen.
4. V. Ueber Händels Julius Cäsar (Kölner Gastspiel); Vortrag der ganzen Sonate abgeschlossen.
7. Schubert Bd II: „Du liebst mich nicht“, Linie.
14. Chopin Nocturne Esdur op. 9 begonnen.

25. S. Bach Präludium Esdur im Anhang der Gesamtausgabe.Diary May 25, 1928: “From noon to 1:30, sanitary inspector Albersheim: a thoroughly humorless person, who does not understand my language, or that of his son. Is it not possible, he asks me, to provide my pupil with a method, which in all instances would suffice for him to get on with on his own? [...] – in the end, he takes the opportunity of saying that he will leave his son here for one more year.”

1. VI. Stimmführungsfragen aus der unvollendeten Fuge Cmoll v. S. Bach (s. Anhang);Diary June 3, 1928: “Work on Bach's Prelude and incomplete Fugue (at Albersheim's request).” Stimmführungsfragen zur Aria variata; vierhändig einige Orgelstücke gespielt.

4. Zum Vortrag von Schuberts
Sinfonie Cdur durch Schalk - Erläuterung der Fehler; Mozart Sonate Adur wiederholt (s. Saison 26–27).
7. Zu Beethovens Octett Esd; Form des 2. u. 3. Satzes; ich spiele mehrere Nocturnes von Chopin vor.
11. Fragen zu anderen Bach-Motetten.

tei:div.tei:note: The lesson reports for Gerhard Albersheim in the original are written continuously, without paragraph breaks or separating punctuation. They have been separated here in the interests of legibility.
tei:div.tei:ab: October 3: Questions about Beethoven’s piano sonatas and String Quartet Op. 18, No. 1.
October 7: Op. 81a principal work to be studied.
October 10: On Beethoven’s Op. 18, No. 1.
October 14: Study of thoroughbass begun.
October 17: Questions about Beethoven’s Op. 59, No. 1, form; on The Marriage of Figaro (suspensions).
October 21: On Beyschlag’s Ornamentation; Beethoven Op. 18, No. 5 (Rosé’s performance); on Schubert’s B minor Symphony.
October 24: Wolf Italian Serenade; Brahms’s Sonata Op. 5; Beethoven Op. 59, No. 1 and No. 2; Reger’s String Quartet, Andante in A major with variations; Op. 81a, first movement, completed.
October 28: A few things about Die Walküre; on the performance of Brahms Op. 117, No. 1.
October 31: On Op. 59, No. 2, No. 3, and the “Harp” Quartet.
November 4: Matters concerning music history, and contemplations of the future in a historical context.
November 7: Metric matters in Op. 59, No. 2 and No. 3.
November 11: J. S. Bach, French Suite in E major begun, graphs for the Allemande.

November 18: On
Beethoven’s Wind Quintet, form and performance; on Beethoven’s Op. 95, form.
November 21: Allemande, final background graphs and performance.
November 25: Brahms Op. 107, No. 5,”Mädchenlied,” the voice-leading line corrected; Götterdämmerung, page 213 (?), keys – questions.
November 28: On Beethoven’s Op. 127 in E major.
December 2: On Meyerbeer’s Le prophète; on Beethoven’s String Quartet in B major; he shows me an essay by Reichwein in the Cologne music journal.
December 5: On Kleiber (in connection with the Strauss concert); Courante begun.
December 9: Schemelli-Roth No. 1 corrected.
December 12: Schemelli-Roth No. 8; Sarabande begun.
December 16: Chorale “Herzliebster Jesu” from the St. Matthew Passion, in B minor.
December 19: Second version (see Erk), also chorales by Mendelssohn and others (published by Peters); chorale preludes and fantasies by J. S. Bach, (see his organ works); the Gavotte begun.

December 23: Thoroughbass finished; a polonaise by Chopin begun;
Cherubino’s aria from The Marriage of Figaro, graph corrected.
December 30: Motet in B major begun; graphs for it.
January 9: The Gigue begun, and thus the French Suite is finished.
January 13: At the visit with Heger, and his verdict. Mozart’s Turkish March, voice-leading line corrected.
January 16: Illness.
January 9: Illness.
January 23: Performance markings written into the motet, in accordance with the results of the voice-leading lines.
January 27: On the Andante music example from Schubert’s G major String Quartet. Ornaments in Schubert’s music.
January 30: On antisemitism, apparently a crisis in his love life.
February 3:Ornamentation in J. S. Bach, questions about my book Ornamentation.
February 10: Questions about Beethoven’s String Quartet Op.135, voice-leading lines for Johann Strauss’s Blue Danube Waltz.
February 13: The motet completed.
February 17: Fugue in E minor from Book I, with graph; Questions about form in Schubert’s piano sonatas.

February 20: On passages from the little monograph by Siegfried Ochs on
the choir.

February 24: Fugue in D minor from Book I; concerning C. P. E. Bach’s embellishments: mordent and Anschlag (double appoggiatura); questions posed, and methodically answered in succession, about the performance of the Suite.

February 27: Performance of some passages from Carmen; concerning horns and trumpets in general; on Furtwängler’s performance of Brahms’s Third Symphony; on Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique; performance of the fugues in C minor from Book I, D minor from Book I, and E minor from Book I, also the corresponding preludes in C minor and E minor.
March 2: C. P. E. Bach: questions about the embellishments, and on the section on performance.
March 5: Brandenburg Concerto in D major begun, the voice-leading line of the first movement.
March 12: Fingering and performance of the French Suite completed. Continuo for the first movement of the Brandenburg Concerto corrected; concerning Mozart’s three-movement Symphony in D major.

March 19: He missed a lesson once again! Sketch for Beethoven’s Eighth Symphony (from Heck) explained; Brandenburg Concerto, second movement, voice-leading line;
Beethoven’s String Quintet in C major, form of the last movement.
March 23: Continuo for the second movement.
March 26: Voice-leading line for the third movement.

April 2: From C. P. E. Bachs last section about appoggiaturas. Brahms’s Sextet in G major; should the diagram of a mordent in the Scherzo be played before or on the beat? Concerning passages from Bach’s Christmas Oratorio, questions of declamation (balance between strong and weak, on the basis of quantity).
April 6: Brandenburg Concerto: performance of the first movement, for the Nicolai Concert.
April 13: Performance of the second and third movements.
April 20: Questions about Bach’s St. John Passion; on Smetana’s The Bartered Bride, 8–8 Stelle; about Smetana and Dvořák generally.

April 23: Concerning variation sets by Schubert in Litolff, vol. III; an aria from a J. S. Bach
cantata, voice-leading line and performance.
April 25: (instead of June 18): Questions about Brahms’s Sextet; once again the voice-leading line for Op. 81a, first movement, gone through and improved.
April 27: On Mozart’s “Linz” Symphony in C major, also played four-hands.
April 30: On Op. 81a, once again the voice-leading line of the Andante, with a methodic beginning to the precise study of its performance.
May 4:Concerning Handel’s Julius Caesar (visiting performance from Cologne); performance of the entire sonata completed.
May 7: Schubert, “Du liebst mich nicht,” from vol. II of the Peters edition, voice-leading line.
May 14:Chopin Nocturne in E major from Op. 9 begun.
May 25: J. S. Bach’s Prelude in E major, in the appendix to the collected edition.

June 1: Questions of voice-leading in the incomplete fugue in C minor by J. S. Bach (see the appendix to the collected edition); questions about voice-leading in the Aria variata; a few organ pieces played four-hands.

June 4: Concerning the performance of Schubert’s
Symphony in C major by Schalk – Explanation of his errors; Mozart Sonata in A major revisited (from the teaching year 1926–27).
June 7: Concerning Beethoven’s Octet in E major, the form of the second and third movements; I play several nocturnes by Chopin to him.
June 11: Questions about other Bach motets.

tei:div.tei:note: The lesson reports for Robert Brünauer in the original are written continuously, without paragraph breaks or separating punctuation. They have been separated here in the interests of legibility.
tei:div.tei:ab: 3. X. Beethoven op. 90 neu, mit Linien.
6. Bach Suite Edur neu, mit Linien.
13. Schreibt alle Schichten der Allemand, mit Tinte!
15. Zeige ihm Vrieslanders Manuscript-Lieder.Cf. Diary Oct 10, 1927: ”To [Otto Erich] Deutsch (postcard): I report with enthusiasm about Vrieslander's songs.”

23. Zur Jause bei uns, spiele mit ihm vierhändig.This records a social occasion, not a lesson: diary Oct 23, 1927: ”From 5 o'clock to 8:15 Dr. Brünauer and Mrs. Bechert, Counselor Pollak and his sister – we gossip about all sorts of things and play even more; Schubert's Divertissement à l'hongrois played for the first time in front of this small gathering.”
7. XI. Ob der 1. Satz von op. 90 - oder -? Gründe.

14. Ist im 1. Satz der Eroica einer Nebennote auf der Spur, die durch das Ganze Paralellismen nach sich zieht; die Beobachtung ist gut: es geht um eine Nebennote im Vordergrunde.Diary Nov 14, 1927: “Brünauer surprises me with an extraordinarily beautiful, visionary observation on the first movement of the “Eroica”: concerning the neighbor note A2, which Beethoven approaches right at the beginning via a hairpin crescendo. He believes that this gesture, this phenomenon in the diminution, may be recognized as being a driving force in the entire work. I agree with him immediately, with the greatest delight, subject to a more detailed examination.” – Cf. Diary Nov 15: “I work on the ‘Eroica.’ The investigation confirms Brünauer's felicitous thought; that Brünauer could hit upon it proves the special fruitfulness of my way of looking at things – it could have occurred to no musician today, because one could arrive at it only by taking my path. Of course, Brünauer would have had to be capable also of finding the more precise explanation, in the way that I have done for myself at his instigation.” – See Ian Bent, Heinrich Schenker and Robert Brünauer: Relations with a Musical Industrialist, in Festschrift Hellmut Federhofer zum 100. Geburtstag, ed. Axel Beer, Gernot Gruber, and Herbert Schneider (Tutzing: Hans Scneider, 2011), pp. 35–36.
17. Sarabande, neu.

21. „An der schönen
blauen Donau“ als --.
28. Rondo op. 90 begonnen.

8. XII. Beethoven-Schindler: zum Vortrag der Sonaten Ed u. Gd als Hilfsquellen für meinen methodisch festgelegten Vortrag;In the first (1840) edition of his Biographie von Ludwig van Beethoven, Anton Felix Schindler provided extensive commentary on the performance of the two sonatas of Op. 14. Gavotte neu.

12. Entrüstet sich über Vrieslanders Brief,Cf. Diary Dec 12, 1927, a long entry beginning: “Brünauer returns to the subject of Vrieslander's letter; he makes angry gestures, is incensed by the ‘impertinence’ that Vrieslander committed in the letter. The hints that he drops lead me to infer that Vrieslander may have reminded him of greater responsibilities toward me. In so doing, he shattered Brünauer's illusion that is his life's lie: [...]” Cf. also Diary Nov 7 and Dec 1, 1927. da er zugleich auch als Mäzen gelten will.
29. Polonaise neu; führe ihm den Stift beim Bildentwurf.
16. I. Gigue, Linie in der Stunde.
30. Aus Schuberts Gdur Quartett, Andante mit obstinatem b2,A play on words: “obstinat”/“ostinato.” vgl. Albersheim u. Hoboken.

6. II. Strauß-Klaiber.Reference is perhaps to the concert by the Vienna Philharmonic under Erich Kleiber that took place on Sunday December 4, 1927. It was not, however, a Strauss concert: the program comprised works by Purcell, Glazunov, and Mahler. Cf. lesson note for January 9.

9. „An der schönen blauen Donau“ – er bringt die Partitur, Kleiber wird bestätigt;Diary Feb 9, 1928: “Brünauer brings to his lesson the score of the "Blue Danube" Waltz, so that I can not only confirm my impression but also see that, retrospectively, justice is done also to Kleiber.” Cf. lesson note for January 6. beginnt den Generalbaß;Diary Feb 9, 1928: “Brünauer asks me to introduce him to thoroughbass.” wiederholt Nocturne Fisdur T. 1–8.
13. Vortrag dieser Nocturne aufs genaueste in jeder Hinsicht.
20. Ueber Hugo Wolf.
23. Rondo op. 90 beendet.

1. III. Fuge Dm I in Angriff genommen; Fragen zu
Mozart Sonate Adur Thema der Variationen u. alla turca.
5. Artikulation der Nocturnes Fd u. Esd.; Mozart: Variation Adagio; über das non legato im alla turca.

8. Noch einmal non legato; über den springenden Durchgang; zeige die Abschrift von op. 90 aus der Hand des Erzherzogs Rudolph.Beethoven’s pupil, Archduke Rudolph of Austria, made a copy of Beethoven’s autograph score of the sonata, probably in 1815 (Austrian National Library, Vienna, Hs. 16.570).

12. Fragen: wo im Ursatz u. den Verwandlungen der Kontrapunkt enthalten ist? Erster Blick auf Chopin Nocturne Desdur, namentlich Zergliederung T. 1–8.Diary March 12, 1928: “[...] during the lesson the opportunity arises for me to explain that music is not merely an object for us to contemplate, but above all a subject of which people still, of course, have not yet the slightest inkling. [...]”
19. Zeige Beethovens Skizze zur VIII. Sinfonie (Heck).
22. Wiederholt die Berçeuse.
26. Fuge bis zur Hälfte gebracht.
29. Zum Schubert-Konzert:Perhaps the Liederabend that evening by Malcolm Davidson and Hilde Schalk in the middle recital room of the Vienna Konzerthaus. Lieder, Streichquartett.
5–30. IV. Zwischen 5–30. IV. Italien
30. IV. Ueber Italien; über die Urlinie im Raum der Malerei u. in der Musik; Erläuterung des Begriffes „Urlinie“.

2. V. (für 21. VI.): Haydn
Sonate Ddur, Adagio Adur.Possibly the Andante of Haydn’s Sonata in D major, Hob. XVI:19. None of Haydn’s other keyboard sonatas in D major has a slow movement in A major.
3. Linien u. Stellen aus den neu erworbenen Händel-Bänden; wiederholt Haydn Menuett Bd.Diary May 3: “During Brünauer's lesson, Hupka appears with Mrs. Kaposi [...]”

7. Möchte das ganze „Wohltemperierte Klavier“ durchgehen, wenn auch flüchtig. Ich lehne das als unausführbar ab; erkläre das ewig-Abänderliche der Fuge als ihr unabänderliches Gesetz; über Julius Cäsar von Händel u. die zwei neuen Em. Bach-Bände „Preussische Sonaten“.Rudolf Steglich’s edition of C. P. E. Bach’s six “Prussian” Sonatas (Wq. 48), published as No. 15 of Nagels Musik-Archiv (Hannover); the foreword to this edition is dated “summer 1927.” Haydn Sonate Ddur 2/4Probably the late Sonata in D major, Hob. XVI:33. gelesen.

9. Ueber den Schubert-Scott-Abend,On May 10, 1928, the Austrian Radio (RAVAG) broadcast a music program with works by Schubert to texts by Walter Scott, accompanied by an "explanatory lecture" by Otto Erich Deutsch, on which Schenker sent Deutsch a postcard on May 14 praising the event. verschiedene Lieder, darunter „Du liebst mich nicht“, Linie.Diary May 9: “Elias and Brünauer for make-up lessons.”
17. Bringt die Linie zum Menuett von Händel-Gdur; liest die Haydn-Sonate Gdur.

21. Wiederholt Stellen aus
der Berçeuse.

23. Zeige Stellen aus Em. Bachs neuen Sonaten.Rudolf Steglich’s edition of the six “Prussian” Sonatas (Wq. 48), published as volume 15 of Nagels Musik-Archiv (Hannover); the foreword to this edition is dated “summer 1927.”

24. Versucht die Linie zu „Sei mir gegrüßt“ von Schubert; Ungarische Melodie, Facsimile (Deutsch).In 1928, the Viennese publishing house of Eduard Strache brought out a hitherto unknown piano solo piece by Schubert, Ungarische Melodie, which was edited by Otto Erich Deutsch.

31. Allgemeines zum Vortrag; liest im „Tonwille“ u. fragt: Wie ist die Nebennote hervorzuheben z.B. in der Nocturne Fisdur oder in Schumanns „Träumerei“; ich wiederhole, daß die Nebennote schon durch die Komposition hervorgehoben, also nicht noch zu unterstreichen sei: in der Nocturne durch das doppio movimento, in der Träumerei durch das Kontrabaß B in der l. H. (von dem er nichts gewußt hat!).
3. VI. Lege die Fragen aus Bach vor (s. Albersheim).See Albersheim’s lesson notes for June 1.

7. Ber-
-çeuse auf seinen Wunsch noch einmal Note für Note.
11. Berçeuse für längere Zeit zurückgelegt.
14. Zeige im Fluge Beethoven 103, Linien aller Sätze.

tei:div.tei:note: The lesson reports for Robert Brünauer in the original are written continuously, without paragraph breaks or separating punctuation. They have been separated here in the interests of legibility.
tei:div.tei:ab: October 3: Beethoven Op. 90 new, with voice-leading lines.
October 6: Bach French Suite in E major new, with voice-leading lines.
October 13: He writes out all the layers of the Allemande, in ink!!
October 15: I show him Vrieslander’s songs in manuscript.
October 23: Late afternoon snack with us; I play piano duets with him.
November 7: Is the first movement of Op. 90 - oder -? Reasons.

November 14: He is on the track of a neighbor-note in the first movement of the “Eroica” Symphony, which invokes parallelisms throughout the movement; the observation is good: it concerns a neighbor-note in the foreground.
November 17: Sarabande, new.

November 21: The Blue Danube Waltz
as --.
November 28: The Rondo from Op. 90 begun.
December 8: Beethoven-Schindler: on the performance of the sonatas in E major and G major as sources aiding my methodically determined performance; Gavotte new.
December 12: He is indignant about Vrieslander’s letter, since he, too, wants to be thought of as a benefactor.
December 29: Polonaise new; I guide his pencil over the drafting of the graph.
January 16: Gigue, the voice-leading line made during the lesson.
January 30: In Schubert’s G major String Quartet, the Andante with the stubborn B2; see the lesson notes for Albersheim and Hoboken.
February 6: Strauss-Klaiber.
February 9: The Blue Danube Waltz – he brings the score, Kleiber is confirmed; he begins the study of thoroughbass; repeats the Nocturne in F major, bars 1–8.
February 13: The performance of this Nocturne, in the greatest detail in every respect.
February 20: On Hugo Wolf.
February 23: The Rondo of Op. 90 finished.

March 1: Fugue in D minor from Book I, taken up; questions about
Mozart’s Sonata in A major, the theme of the variations and of the Turkish March.
March 5: Articulation of the nocturnes in F major and E major; Mozart, Adagio variation; concerning the non legato in the Turkish March.
March 8: Once again, non legato; on the leaping passing tone; I show him the copy of Op. 90 in Archduke Rudolph’s hand.
March 12: Questions: where is counterpoint conveyed in the Ursatz and the voice-leading transformations? First glimpse of Chopin’s Nocturne in D major, especially the analysis of bars 1–8.
March 19: I show him Beethoven’s sketch for the Eighth Symphony (from Heck).
March 22: Revisit of the Berceuse.
March 26: The first half of the fugue performed.
March 29: On the Schubert concert: songs, string quartet.
April 5–30: In Italy between April 5 and April 30.
April 30: About Italy; concerning the Urlinie in the field of painting and in music; elucidation of the concept of Urlinie.

May 2: (in place of June 21). Haydn
Sonata in D major, Adagio in A major.
May 3: Voice-leading lines and passages from the newly acquired volumes of Handel; Haydn’s Minuet in B major revisited.

May 7: He would like to go through the Well-tempered Clavier in its entirety, even if hastily so. I reject that as impracticable; I explain that the ever-variable nature of the fugue is its immutable law; on Handel’s Julius Caesar and the two new volumes of C. P. E. Bach’s “Prussian” Sonatas. He reads Haydn’s Sonata in D major with the first movement in 2/4 time.
May 9: On the Schubert-Scott evening, various songs, including “Du liebst mich nicht,” voice-leading line.
May 17: He brings the voice-leading line of Handel’s Minuet in G major; he reads Haydn’s Sonata in G major.

May 21: Passages from
the Berceuse revisited.
May 23: I show him passages from C. P. E. Bach’s newly published sonatas.
May 24: He attempts the voice-leading line of Schubert’s “Sei mir gegrüßt”; Hungarian Melody, facsimile (Deutsch).

May 31: General matters concerning performance; he reads from Der Tonwille and asks me how to bring out the neighbor-note, for example, in the Nocturne in F major or in Schumann’s Träumerei; I repeat that the neighbor-note is already brought out by the composition itself and is thus not to be emphasized: in the Nocturne, by the doppio movimento; in Träumerei, by the low bass B in the left hand (of which he knew nothing!).
June 3: I set out the questions from Bach (see Albersheim).

June 7: The Berceuse
once again, note for note, at his request.
June 11: The Berceuse set aside for an extended period of time.
June 14: I quickly show him the voice-leading lines for all the movements of Beethoven’s Op. 10, No. 3.

tei:div.tei:note: The lesson reports for Angi Elias in the original are written continuously, without paragraph breaks or separating punctuation. They have been separated here in the interests of legibility.
tei:div.tei:ab: 1. X. Liest Haydn Bd.Probably the Sonata in B major, Hob. XVI:41, which however appeared in vol. 3 of some early 20th-century German editions of the Haydn keyboard sonatas. aus Heft IV.Diary Oct 1, 1927: “Miss Elias raises her lesson payments to 50 shillings by paying an extra $270, something that I of course refuse since it far exceeds 50 shillings.” – Elias frequently raised Schenker’s fee voluntarily.
4. Bach Suite Ed, neu.

6. Zeige Schindlers ErstdruckSchenker is referring to the first edition of Anton Felix Schindler’s Beethoven biography (1840), which includes extensive commentary on the performance of these sonatas. zu 141 u. 2.
13. S. Bach: Menuet Cm, Händel zugeschrieben, korrigiere das Bild.
15. Zeige die neuen Vrieslander-Lieder.Cf. Diary Oct 10: “To [Otto Erich] Deutsch (postcard): I report with enthusiasm about Vrieslander's songs.”
20. Linie zu Mendelssohns Frühlingslied nachträglich corrigiert.

22. Wiederhole die Schindler-ErgebnisseAnton Felix Schindler’s commentary on the performance of Beethoven’s two Op. 14 sonatas, in the first edition of his Beethoven biography (1840). – There is no reference to Schindler or his findings in Marianne Kahn’s lesson notes at this time. ausdrücklich für Frl. Kahn.

29. In Heft IV fortfahrend Sonate Dd gelesen.Probably Haydn’s Keyboard Sonata in D major, Hob. XVI:42, which usually follows the Sonata in B, Hob. XVI: 41, in printed editions. See the October 1 lessonbook entry for Elias.

3. XI. Zeige die erste Fassung von 181; die Revisions-Ergebnisse in Schubert Sinfonie Hm von Brahms u. mir.Sometime in the 1890s, Schenker copied Brahms’s textual corrections to Schubert’s “Unfinished” Symphony into his personal copy of the score and made further observations on divergences between the autograph score and the published editions. At the invitation of Alfred Kalmus, general editor of the Wiener Philharmonischer Verlag, he worked further on this project in the autumn of 1927, with assistance from Otto Erich Deutsch. A new edition of the score was duly published in April 1928, but without any credit given to Schenker, Brahms, or Deutsch.

5. Beleuchte die
Fehler von Frl. Kahn im Vortrag der Sonate op. 23, 14 u. 22, 1. Satz.Angi Elias and Marianne Kahn were close friends. – Cf. Kahn’s lesson notes for November 5 (in which no mention is made of errors).

15. Ueber den Vortrag von Dohnany u. Rosenthal im Rf.;According to the radio program listings of the Neue freie Presse, recitals by Ernst Dohnanyi and Moriz Rosenthal were broadcast on November 11 and 12, respectively. Sarabande neu.
22. Gavotte neu.Diary Nov 23: “To Miss Elias (express postcard): I ask her to bring Op. 107 by Brahms with her (on account of a Mädchenlied for Albersheim).”

24. „An der schönen blauen Donau“ Bild corrigiert.Brünauer had brought the score of the waltz to his lesson with Schenker on February 9, 1928. But the Urlinie of the waltz had already been discussed in Brünauer’s lesson on November 21. – Diary Nov 23: “To Miss Elias (express postcard): I ask her to bring Op. 107 by Brahms with her (on account of a Mädchenlied for Albersheim).” – Cf. Albersheim’s lesson notes for Nov 25, 1927.
26. Haydn Cd, Eintragungen nach André aus Hobokens Sammlung.

29. Ueber den Brief Vrieslanders an sie; corrigiere ihre Verbesserungen einiger Takte ihres Neffen Peter.Diary Nov 29: “Miss Elias reports about a letter to her from Vrieslander; I instruct her to send Vrieslander a few addresses.”
3. XII. Spielt Haydn Cd.
6. Gavotte.
13. Polonaise, Bild corrigiert.

22. Einblick in Toch’s Melodielehre; über Messchaerts Kunst.Ernst Toch, Melodielehre (Berlin: Hesse, 1923). – Diary Dec 20: ”Miss Elias brings me a book, Gesangstunde bei Messchaert, which has just been published; even a quick glance is sufficient to confirm its correctness. In earlier years, I often used to talk about individual features of his great artistry; they have been reproduced in the most faithful way in this little book.”
24. Haydn Sonate Gd.
29. Nachträglich Vortragsbemerkungen zu den Ungarischen Tänzen.

31. Brahms Se-
-renade Ad, 1. Satz, zum Vortrag.This may have been Brahms’s arrangement of the Serenade for piano four hands, which Elias may have wanted to play with her friend Marianne Kahn.

tei:div.tei:ab: October 1: She reads Haydn’s Sonata in B major from volume 4.
October 4: Bach French Suite in E major, new.
October 6I show her Schindler’s first edition on Op. 14, No. 1 and No. 2.
October 13: J. S. Bach’s Minuet in C minor, attributed to Handel; I correct the graph.
October 15: I show her the new songs by Vrieslander.
October 20:Voice-leading line for Mendelssohn’s “Spring Song”, subsequently corrected.
October 22: I revisit the findings of Schindler expressly for Miss Kahn.
October 29: Continuing in volume 4, the sonata in D major read.
November 3: I show her the first version of Op.18, No. 1 and the results of the revision of Schubert’s Symphony in B minor, made by Brahms and me.

November 5: I illuminate the
errors made by Frl. Kahn in the performance of the first movement of the sonatas Op. 2, No. 3, Op. 14 and Op. 22
November 22: Gavotte, new.
November 24: The Blue Danube Waltz, the graph corrected.
November 26: Haydn Sonata in C major, annotations based on André’s edition in Hoboken’s private collection.
November 29: About Vrieslander's letter to her; I correct her improvements of several bars of her nephew Peter.
December 3: She plays Haydn’s Sonata in C major.
December 6: Gavotte.
December 13: Polonaise, the graph corrected.
December 22: Glimpse of Toch’s Theory of Melody; on Messchaert’s art.
December 24: Haydn Sonata in G major.
December 27: Bourrée; Brahms’s Hungarian Dances, played four-hands.
December 29: Retrospective remarks on the performance of Brahms’s Hungarian Dances.

December 31: Brahms's
Serenade in A major, first movement, for performance.
